props.title: Rogue
props.initialSlug: Giant killer croc hunts tourists in Australia

sections.content: Rogue stands as one of the most effective creature features to emerge from Australia, following the success of Wolf Creek (2005) in establishing Greg McLean as a formidable horror director. The film draws from the same vein as classic killer crocodile films like Dark Age (1987) and Alligator (1980), but elevates the formula through stunning Northern Territory cinematography and a surprisingly patient approach to building tension. McLean deliberately echoes Jaws (1975) in his restrained reveal of the monster, using the beautiful but menacing landscape to create a sense of isolation and vulnerability.

sections.content: What sets Rogue apart is its commitment to character development before unleashing chaos. Unlike lesser entries in the genre like Primeval (2007) or Lake Placid 2 (2007), McLean takes time to establish Michael Vartan's American travel writer and Radha Mitchell's tour guide as fully realized characters. The film's first act mirrors Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975) in its ethereal appreciation of Australia's natural beauty, making the eventual descent into terror more impactful.

The practical effects work in Rogue deserves special mention, combining animatronics with CGI in a way that holds up remarkably well. This hybrid approach recalls the best elements of Anaconda (1997) while avoiding its campier elements. The crocodile's design emphasizes realistic behavior over spectacle, drawing from actual saltwater crocodile incidents in Australia's Northern Territory for authenticity. sections.content: Rogue helped cement Australia's reputation for uncompromising natural horror, paving the way for films like The Reef (2010) and Bait 3D (2012). Its success demonstrated that regional horror could compete internationally while maintaining cultural specificity, similar to how Razorback (1984) had done decades earlier with its distinctly Australian take on the killer animal genre.
